description: Apple scab is a common fungal disease of plants in the Rosaceae family, particularly Malus species (apple and crabapple). It causes dark, irregular lesions on leaves, blossoms, and fruits, leading to fruit deformation, premature leaf and fruit drop, and potential crop losses up to 70%. The disease rarely kills the host but reduces yield and quality significantly.
symptoms_and_damage: Leaves: velvety-brown to olive-green spots with distinct margins, often cupping underside of leaf
Older leaves: raised dark-green to gray-brown lesions causing cupping and leaf curl
Fruits: small black spots that become brown, corky, and scabby
Increases susceptibility to secondary infections and abiotic stress
disease_cycle: Overwinters in leaf litter and infected plant debris as pseudothecia
Early spring: cool, moist conditions trigger release of sexual ascospores
Spores are spread by wind and splashing water to leaves and blossoms
Tissue penetration occurs via germ tube or appressorium
Light-green lesions develop, darken, and expand; fruit lesions become corky
Within 10 days, asexual conidia form for secondary infections
Cycle may repeat every 1–2 weeks under favorable conditions
At season end, infected leaves and fruit fall, forming pseudothecia for next season
favorable_conditions: Cool and moist weather during spore release
Dense tree canopy that slows leaf drying
prevention_and_cultural_controls: Select sunny planting sites to improve air circulation
Remove and destroy fruit drops, leaf litter, and prunings to reduce inoculum
Regular pruning to open canopy for rapid drying
After harvest, apply 5% urea solution prior to leaf fall to accelerate decomposition
Avoid overhead irrigation during spore release periods
chemical_control: Spray Mancozeb @ 2 g/l of water, repeat 2–3 times at 7-day intervals; WHO Class U, PHI 14–28 days, FRAC MO3
Spray Carbendazim 50% WP @ 2 g/l at early flowering; WHO Class U, PHI 14 days
Follow product label instructions, rotate modes of action to prevent resistance
biological_control: Bacillus subtilis @ 50 ml/ropani (e.g., Serenade Opti) before/during rainy season
Trichoderma harzianum 100 ml/ropani under high-risk conditions
Fungal antagonist Cladosporium cladosporioides strain H39 reduces leaf scab 42–98% and fruit scab 41–94%
resistance_breeding: PRI Apple Breeding Program developed 1500 resistant cultivars; examples: 'Prima', 'Jonafree', 'Goldrush'
Fifteen resistance genes identified; Vf (Rvi6) gene widely studied
Resistance genes derived from wild Malus spp. in East Asia
Potential for transgenic cultivars, but adoption is limited due to market acceptance and pathogen evolution
monitoring: Inspect leaves for velvety-brown to olive-green spots
Monitor older leaves for raised gray-brown lesions
Check fallen leaves for curled and shriveled tissue
Observe fruits for black spots developing into scabs
direct_control_and_restrictions: Remove and dispose of severely infected plant parts in a pit at least 30 cm deep
Prune trees to improve leaf drying after rain
Wear protective clothing when using pesticides
Avoid repeated use of chemicals with same mode of action
sources: PRI Apple Breeding Program, Purdue University, Rutgers University, University of Illinois
